title: Elements with role="img" need a text label
summary: An element marked role="img" has no accessible name, so a screen reader has nothing to announce. Add an aria-label that says what it shows.
problem: An element such as a <span> or <div> has role="img", which tells assistive technology to treat it as a picture. It has no aria-label, aria-labeledby or title, so the picture has no name. This is common with icon fonts and emoji.
whoItAffects: Screen reader users are told there is an image but not what it shows, or the element is skipped. A star rating, a status icon or a warning symbol then conveys nothing to them.
steps: Find elements with role="img" in your templates. The scan result shows the exact markup.
Add an aria-label that says what the picture means, such as aria-label="Rated 4 out of 5 stars".
If the picture sits next to visible text that already says the same thing, remove role="img" and add aria-hidden="true" so it is skipped.
Keep the label short and describe the meaning, not the shape.
whyItMatters: Non-text content needs a text alternative under WCAG 1.1.1, a Level A criterion. Without one, information such as a customer rating or a status icon is available only to people who can see it.
howToCheck: Open the browser accessibility inspector, select the element and read its Name. An empty Name on an element with role img means the label is missing.
